s: The children of Israel, also called Jacob, are the people brought out of Egypt by the LORD's might, organized into tribes and fathers' houses each headed by a prince, and bound to the LORD by command and law. The records open at Sinai, where they are counted at 603,550 fighting men and told to encamp each by his own standard around the Tent of Meeting, at a distance from it. They obey the LORD's commands: putting the unclean outside the camp, keeping Passover in the first month, and traveling or camping by the cloud. The Levites are taken in place of their firstborn to serve and make atonement, and the people may not approach the Tent of Meeting lest they bear sin and die, a fear they voice themselves. They depart Sinai in the second year in ordered tribal divisions. The journey is marked by repeated complaint: weeping for the food of Egypt (fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, garlic), fire at Taberah, plague at Kibroth Hattaavah, then Hazeroth, where they wait for Miriam, and the wilderness of Paran. They wish to return to Egypt, threaten Joshua and Caleb, and are sentenced to wander forty years, with the dead falling in the wilderness. They presume to attack and are beaten to Hormah. They are given offering laws, the red heifer statute (one law for them and the stranger), and are punished with snakes and healed by the bronze serpent. They then defeat Sihon and Og and possess their lands. In the plains of Moab, Balaam cannot curse them: God declares them blessed, a people dwelling alone, strong as a wild ox, like a lioness and lion, with a king among them, no enchantment against them, and a future star and scepter rising from them. Those who bless them are blessed and those who curse them are cursed. Yet at Shittim they join Baal Peor, provoking the LORD's anger and a plague of twenty-four thousand until Phinehas acts. A second census counts 601,730, with none of the earlier generation remaining except Caleb and Joshua. The book closes with festival offerings, vengeance on Midian, Reuben and Gad's pledge, the journey recounted from Egypt under Moses and Aaron, and commands to drive out Canaan's inhabitants, allot the land by lot, give the Levites cities in proportion, appoint cities of refuge, and keep inheritances within tribes.

A census of Israel, conducted by Moses with Aaron, counts males twenty and older able to go to war by families and fathers' houses, tribe by tribe, from Reuben to Naphtali. Judah is largest at 74,600; Levi is excluded by the LORD's command. The total is 603,550.

Reuben, firstborn of Israel, is a tribe led by Elizur and counted at 46,500 fighting men (43,730 in families). Owning vast livestock, Reuben and Gad request land east of the Jordan, promise to cross armed ahead of Israel, and are granted it, then rebuild cities, renaming some.

Gad is a tribal group led by prince Eliasaph, counted at 45,650 fighting men (also listed as 40,500). With Reuben and their great livestock, they request land east of the Jordan, promise to fight armed before Israel, receive it, and build fortified cities and sheepfolds including Dibon, Ataroth, Aroer and Jazer.

The Levites are a tribe set apart by the LORD and deliberately excluded from the census of the children of Israel, because they receive no inheritance of land among them. Their central significance is that they belong to the LORD, taken in place of Israel's firstborn, and are given to Aaron and his sons as a gift dedicated to the LORD to serve in the Tent of Meeting. The records first establish their appointment as custodians of the Tabernacle of the Testimony: they carry it with its furnishings, take it down, set it up, and encamp around it so no wrath falls on the congregation. They camp in the middle of the camps, and the Tent of Meeting sets out with them. They are then set before Aaron, and 22,000 males from a month old are counted across the three clans of Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Those aged thirty to fifty who enter service number 8,580, each assigned his service and burden. Wagons and oxen are distributed by service: Gershon receives two wagons and four oxen, Merari four wagons and eight oxen under Ithamar, while Kohath receives none because they carry the holy things on their shoulders. The Levites are cleansed and offered as a wave offering, serving from age twenty-five and retiring at fifty, after which they assist their brothers. Their duties carry limits and costs: they make atonement so no plague strikes when Israel approaches the sanctuary, but they must not approach the altar or the sanctuary vessels on pain of death, and they bear their own iniquity. In place of land they receive Israel's tithe as inheritance by a statute forever, and they give a tithe of the tithe to Aaron the priest. A later count lists the families, including Libnites, Hebronites, Mahlites, Mushites, and Korahites, totaling 23,000 males from a month old. The records end with the provision of forty-eight cities with pasture lands, six of them cities of refuge, given out of Israel's inheritance for the Levites to dwell in.

Nahshon, son of Amminadab of the tribe of Judah, offered first on the first day of the altar's dedication, presenting silver platter and bowl of flour and oil, a golden ladle of incense, and animal offerings.

l: princes (heads of the thousands of Israel), Numbers
s: The princes are twelve tribal leaders, each head of his fathers' house, also called heads of the thousands of Israel. In Chapter 1, one man from each tribe, from Elizur of Reuben to Ahira of Naphtali, is named to stand with Moses and Aaron and assist in the counting. In Chapter 7, as overseers of those counted, they bring six covered wagons and twelve oxen, then each gives an identical altar dedication offering on successive days: silver platters, silver bowls, golden ladles, and sacrificial animals.

The Tabernacle of the Testimony, also called the Tent of the Testimony, is a sacred tent entrusted to the Levites, who carry its furnishings, take it down, set it up, and encamp around it; any stranger approaching is to be put to death, and their encampment guards the congregation from wrath. When it was raised, the cloud covered it. The cloud resting on or lifting from it decides whether Israel camps or travels. When the cloud lifts, Gershon's and Merari's sons carry it, and others set it up before the Kohathites arrive.

The camp of Judah, with Issachar and Zebulun, encamps on the east side toward the sunrise under prince Nahshon. Totaling 186,400 across its divisions, it holds the lead position, setting out first in the march order.
Camp of Reuben is a tribal division encamped on the south side, led by prince Elizur son of Shedeur, combining Reuben, Simeon and Gad; totaling 151,450 by armies, it sets out second in the march.

The camp of Ephraim, led by prince Elishama, includes Manasseh and Benjamin and encamps on the west side. Its divisions total 108,100 (Ephraim 40,500, Manasseh 32,200, Benjamin 35,400), and it sets out third in march order.

The camp of Dan is a three-tribe division (Dan, Asher, Naphtali) encamped on the north side under prince Ahiezer son of Ammishaddai; totaling 157,600 men, it is the largest-numbered camp noted and marches last.

l: census count of the tribes, Numbers
s: total_count 603,550 [all counted of the camps according to their armies] Each tribe's division is given a count, from 32,200 for Manasseh to 74,600 for Judah. The camp totals are 186,400, 151,450, 108,100, and 157,600, and all counted of the camps came to 603,550, with the Levites excluded.

l: order of encampment and march, Numbers
s: march_sequence Judah, Reuben, Tent of Meeting with Levites, Ephraim, Dan [as they encamp, so they set out] Judah is on the east, Reuben on the south, Ephraim on the west, and Dan on the north, around the Tent of Meeting. They march in the order Judah, Reuben, the Tent of Meeting with the Levites, Ephraim, and Dan last, and as they encamp, so they set out, each man in his place.

Eleazar is a priest, a son of Aaron, and a prince of the Levites' princes with oversight of those who keep the sanctuary requirements. His duties include the oil for the light, sweet incense, continual meal offering, anointing oil, and the tabernacle's requirements. He appears early in the account taking the censers from the burning, scattering the fire, and beating the bronze censers into an altar covering as a memorial that no outsider to Aaron's line may burn incense. He then receives the red heifer, sprinkles its blood seven times toward the Tent of Meeting, and watches it burned. On the plains of Moab he conducts the census with Moses, his brothers Nadab and Abihu having died for strange fire. He is designated to inquire by the Urim for Joshua, before whom Joshua is commissioned. After the battle he tells the soldiers the purification statute, receives the LORD's wave offering from the warriors' half, and brings the officers' gold into the Tent of Meeting. He succeeds Aaron, receiving his garments, and is named with Joshua to divide Canaan.

The sons of Aaron are priests who serve alongside Aaron. They blow Moses' silver trumpets by a statute forever across generations, then share the priesthood, the altar and veil duties, and a perpetual portion of holy things, with males eating the most holy things and daughters sharing wave offerings.

The firstborn of Israel, both man and animal, belong to the LORD, made holy when he struck down Egypt's firstborn. Males from a month old number 22,273, and the Levites replace them. Firstborn men are redeemed for five shekels; cows, sheep and goats are holy, not redeemed.

The Gershonites are a Levite family division, the sons of Gershon, descending through Libni and Shimei into the Libnite and Shimeite families. They number 7,500 males from a month old and camp west behind the tabernacle under prince Eliasaph. Their duty is the tabernacle curtains, coverings, screens, hangings and cords. Later, 2,630 men aged thirty to fifty carry these under Ithamar's direction, receiving two wagons and four oxen.

The Kohathites are a Levite family division, sons of Levi descending from Kohath through Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. They number 8,600 males and camp on the tabernacle's south side under prince Elizaphan. Their duty is the ark, table, lamp stand, altars, and sanctuary vessels, under Eleazar's oversight. They carry the most holy things on their shoulders, without wagons, after Aaron and his sons cover them, and must not touch or see them. 2,750 men aged thirty to fifty serve.

The Merarites are a Levite group descending from Merari through Mahli and Mushi, forming the Mahlite and Mushite families. They number 6,200 males from a month old and camp on the tabernacle's north side under prince Zuriel son of Abihail. Their duty is the tabernacle's boards, bars, pillars, sockets, pins, cords and court pillars. Serving under Ithamar, 3,200 men aged thirty to fifty carry these items, receiving four wagons and eight oxen for their service.

counts males from a month old and upward [Levi's sons by fathers' houses and families] At the LORD's command Moses counts every Levite male from a month old and upward by fathers' houses and families. The clans total seven thousand five hundred Gershonites, eight thousand six hundred Kohathites, and six thousand two hundred Merarites, twenty-two thousand in all.

Redemption of the 273 surplus firstborn Israelites exceeding the Levites: the LORD sets a price of five sanctuary shekels each, Moses collects 1,365 shekels in total, and gives the money to Aaron and his sons.

A census of Levite men aged thirty to fifty entering Tent of Meeting service, conducted by Moses, Aaron and the princes at the LORD's command: 2,750 Kohathites, 2,630 Gershonites, 3,200 Merarites, totaling 8,580.

assigned_by Moses [each according to his service and burden, as the LORD commanded] Duties are divided by clan: the Kohathites carry the covered holy furnishings, the Gershonites the curtains and hangings, and the Merarites the structural frame parts. Eleazar oversees the oil, incense, and offerings, Ithamar oversees the Gershonites and Merarites, and each man is assigned his own burden.
The camp is the place in the midst of which the LORD dwells, and it must not be defiled. Lepers, those with a discharge, and those unclean by a corpse, male and female, are put outside it.

l: unclean persons (lepers, those with discharge, those defiled by a corpse), Numbers
s: Unclean persons, male and female, including lepers, are ordered outside the camp to avoid defiling it, and the Israelites obey and carry this out.

receives heave offerings [all holy things presented to him] The priest receives restitution when the wronged party has no kinsman, along with the ram of atonement, and the holy things and heave offerings brought to him are his. In the jealousy ordeal he brings the woman before the LORD, prepares the holy water with dust from the tabernacle floor, looses her hair, administers the oath, writes the curses in a book and washes them into the water, waves the meal offering, burns a handful on the altar, and makes her drink the water.

A wife under her jealous husband's authority, suspected of unfaithfulness, is brought to the priest, swears an oath, says "Amen, Amen," and drinks the water of bitterness. Guilt brings swelling, a fallen thigh and a curse; innocence brings freedom and conception.

is_free_from iniquity [under the law of jealousy] The husband, on whom the spirit of jealousy has come, brings his wife to the priest with her offering of barley meal. He sets her before the LORD for the priest to carry out the law. He is declared free from iniquity.

Restitution for trespass against the LORD requires confessing the sin and repaying in full plus a fifth to the one wronged; if he has no kinsman, payment goes to the LORD and belongs to the priest, besides the atonement ram.

applies_to wife (suspected wife) [when she goes astray and is defiled, or when husband suspects her] This law applies when a husband is jealous of his wife, whether or not she is defiled, and there is no witness. He sets her before the LORD, and the priest carries out the whole procedure on her. It leaves the husband free from iniquity and the wife to bear her own.

A meal offering of jealousy: one tenth of an ephah of barley meal without oil or frankincense, called a memorial offering that brings iniquity to memory. The woman holds it, the priest waves it, burns a handful, then gives her water.

Water of bitterness is holy water in an earthen vessel mixed with tabernacle floor dust and the priest's written curses. A woman drinks it after an oath: if defiled it turns bitter, swelling her body and making her thigh fall away; if clean, it does no harm.

is_sworn_by wife (suspected wife) [priest administers; she answers Amen, Amen] The priest has the woman swear this oath, declaring that if she has been defiled the LORD will make her a curse and an oath among her people, with her thigh falling away and her body swelling. The woman answers "Amen, Amen."

The Nazirite is a person who vows separation to the LORD. Throughout the days of separation he is holy, abstains from wine and grape products, lets his hair grow, and avoids dead bodies, even those of his father, mother, brother, or sister. If suddenly defiled by a death, he shaves, brings offerings, and loses the former days. At the vow's end he is brought to the Tent of Meeting, offers a lamb, ewe lamb, ram, and bread, shaves, burns the hair under the peace offerings, and may then drink wine.

is_a special vow [made by man or woman] The Nazirite vow is a special vow, open to man or woman, of separation to the LORD for a set period. It requires abstaining from grape products, leaving the hair uncut, and avoiding the dead, and the person must do according to the vow made, in addition to what he can afford.

receives wave offering portions [breast, thigh, shoulder, cake, wafer] The priest offers the sin offering and burnt offering to atone for a Nazirite defiled by a death. At the completion of the vow he presents the offerings, offers the ram and its meal and drink offerings, and waves the boiled shoulder, cake, and wafer, which are holy for the priest along with the breast and thigh.

Two turtledoves or young pigeons, one for a sin offering and one for a burnt offering, plus a male lamb as a trespass offering, are required when a Nazirite is defiled. At the end of the vow, the Nazirite brings a male lamb, an ewe lamb, a ram for peace offerings, unleavened bread, wafers, and meal and drink offerings.

The priestly blessing is the LORD's prescribed three-line benediction for Aaron and his sons to speak over Israel. It asks him to bless and keep, shine his face and be gracious, and lift his face and give peace, placing his name on them.
The altar had been anointed and sanctified with all its vessels. The twelve princes gave offerings for its dedication on the day it was anointed, each on his own appointed day before the altar.

l: wagons and oxen (offering of the princes), Numbers
s: consists_of six covered wagons and twelve oxen [a wagon for every two princes, an ox for each] The princes brought six covered wagons and twelve oxen before the tabernacle, a wagon for every two princes and an ox for each. The LORD told Moses to accept them for the service of the Tent of Meeting, and Moses distributed them to the Levites by their service.

l: dedication offerings of the altar, Numbers
s: The twelve princes of Israel each offered identical dedication gifts of the altar on twelve successive days: a silver platter, silver bowl, golden ladle, and animals for burnt, sin, and peace offerings. Together these totaled 2,400 silver shekels, 120 gold shekels, and the listed livestock.

includes sprinkling with water of cleansing [also shaving the whole body and washing clothes] The LORD commands that the Levites be cleansed by sprinkling water of cleansing, shaving their whole bodies, and washing their clothes, along with bull offerings. The Levites purify themselves and wash their clothes, and Aaron makes atonement for them, as the LORD commanded.

is_performed_by Aaron [offers the Levites before the LORD] The Levites are to be offered as a wave offering before the LORD by Aaron, on behalf of the children of Israel, so that they may do the LORD's service. Aaron does this after the Levites are cleansed, setting them apart as the LORD's.

The Passover is a LORD-appointed observance kept on the fourteenth day of the first month at evening, under statutes forbidding leaving any until morning or breaking a bone. Israel keeps it in the wilderness of Sinai. A second-month alternative is allowed, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. A clean man not on a journey who neglects it is cut off, while a foreigner may keep it by the same statute. The feast of unleavened bread follows on the fifteenth.

l: unclean men (Israelites defiled by a dead body), Numbers
s: is_unclean_because_of dead body (of a man, defiling the unclean men) Certain men, unclean because of the dead body of a man, could not keep the Passover on its day. They came before Moses and Aaron and asked why they were kept back from offering the LORD's offering in its season among the children of Israel. Their question leads the LORD to provide for a second-month Passover.

The cloud is a guiding presence over the tabernacle (Tent of the Testimony). It covers it from the day it is raised, appearing as fire at night, continually. Its lifting signals Israel to travel; where it rests, they camp, for a night, days, a month, or a year. It lifts on the twentieth day of the second month of the second year, then stays in the wilderness of Paran, over the people by day.

l: Israel's travel and encampment guided by the cloud, Numbers
s: Israel's wilderness movement is governed by the LORD's commandment through the cloud over the tabernacle: they travel when it lifts and encamp where it remains, for a night, days, a month or a year, obediently keeping the LORD's command.

A provision for a second-month Passover, answering the complaint of men made unclean by a dead body or away on a distant journey. In every generation they keep it on the fourteenth day of the second month at evening, eating unleavened bread and bitter herbs, leaving none until morning and breaking no bone, unlike a clean man at home, who is cut off if he neglects it.

Two trumpets of beaten silver, made by Moses, serve to call the congregation and direct the camps' journeying. Blowing both gathers everyone at the Tent of Meeting, one gathers the princes, and an alarm sends the camps forward. They also sound alarms in war and are blown over offerings on gladness days, feasts, and months' beginnings.

Hobab, son of Reuel the Midianite and Moses' father-in-law, is invited by Moses to join Israel. He first refuses, preferring his own land and relatives. Moses asks again, citing his wilderness knowledge and promising shared good.

l: ark of the LORD’s covenant, Numbers
s: goes_before Israel [three days’ journey, seeking a resting place] The ark goes before Israel three days' journey from the Mount of the LORD to seek out a resting place for them. When it goes forward, Moses calls on the LORD to rise and scatter his enemies, and when it rests, he asks the LORD to return to the thousands of Israel.

Israel's departure from the wilderness of Sinai, begun in the second year, second month, on the twentieth day when the cloud lifted, at the LORD's command by Moses. The tribes march in set order, Judah first and Dan, Asher and Naphtali as rear guard, with the tabernacle and sanctuary carried between, while the ark leads three days' journey.

Manna is a food resembling coriander seed and bdellium, falling on the camp with night dew. The people ground, beat, boiled and made it into cakes, tasting like fresh oil, yet they complain of seeing nothing else.

The people crave meat, and the LORD promises to give it to them for a whole month until it comes out of their nostrils and is loathsome. Moses doubts that flocks, herds or all the fish of the sea could supply it. The meat is provided as quails, and the LORD strikes the people with a plague while it is still between their teeth.

A wind from the LORD brings quails from the sea and drops them around the camp, about a day's journey in each direction and about two cubits above the ground. The people gather them for a day, a night and another day, with the least gatherer collecting ten homers, and spread them out around the camp.

Seventy elders of Israel, officers over the people, are gathered by Moses at the Tent of Meeting and appointed by the LORD to share the people's burden; they receive Spirit taken from Moses, prophesy once, and do not again.
Eldad is a man listed among those written who stays in the camp instead of going to the Tent; the Spirit rests on him, he prophesies there, and a young man reports it to Moses.
Medad is a man listed among those written who stays in the camp rather than going to the Tent; the Spirit rests on him and he prophesies, prompting Joshua to ask Moses to forbid them.

Joshua, son of Nun of the tribe of Ephraim, was originally named Hoshea until Moses called him Joshua. He is first one of the twelve spies sent into Canaan. With Caleb he tears his clothes, urges the congregation not to rebel or fear, and is threatened with stoning. He and Caleb are the only adults of that generation who will enter the Promised Land, and he survives when the other spies die. The LORD names him a man in whom is the Spirit and appoints him to succeed Moses, with the laying on of hands before Eleazar and the congregation. He follows the LORD completely, consults Eleazar by the Urim, and is appointed with Eleazar to divide the land of Canaan.
A plague struck Israel after the people joined Baal Peor, killed twenty-four thousand, and ended when Phinehas speared Zimri and Cozbi.

The LORD takes some of the Spirit that is on Moses and puts it on the seventy elders, and they prophesy when it rests on them. The Spirit also rests on Eldad and Medad in the camp, and Moses wishes the LORD would put his Spirit on all his people.

Miriam, a person, joined Aaron in speaking against Moses over his Cushite wife, was rebuked and struck with leprosy, shut outside the camp seven days until restored, and later died and was buried at Kadesh.

Miriam's leprosy, white as snow, struck after the LORD's anger over her and Aaron's sin against Moses. When the cloud lifted, Aaron pleaded and Moses asked healing; the LORD ordered seven days outside the camp, then readmission.

l: Miriam and Aaron's sin against Moses, Numbers
s: Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses over his Cushite wife, questioning whether the LORD spoke only through him. The LORD heard, rebuked them, and his anger burned. Aaron acknowledged it as a foolish sin, and Miriam was struck with leprosy and shut outside the camp seven days.

Twelve men, each a prince of his tribe, are sent to explore Canaan and return after forty days with fruit and a report. They agree the land is rich, but ten declare the people too strong, spreading an evil report that makes the congregation murmur against Moses. Those ten die by plague; only Joshua and Caleb survive.

l: Caleb the son of Jephunneh, Numbers
s: Caleb, son of Jephunneh of the tribe of Judah, is one of the twelve spies and a prince representing Judah. After the spies' report he stills the people and urges them to possess the land, saying Israel is well able to overcome it. He tears his clothes and, with Joshua, urges trust in the LORD rather than fear. The LORD names him his servant, with another spirit who followed fully, and promises he will enter the land, his offspring possessing it. He survives the plague that kills the other spies.

The Israelites are the people promised the land, each tribe sending a spy. At Kadesh they hear Caleb's call to conquer alongside the other spies' evil report. Rebellion follows: some join the rebels, the rest flee as the earth swallows them, then the congregation blames Moses and Aaron, and a plague kills 14,700 until Aaron's atonement stops it. Back at Kadesh in Zin they quarrel over water and food, drink from the rock, are refused passage by Edom, and mourn Aaron thirty days at Mount Hor. Finally, with Moses praying for a shepherd, they are told to obey Joshua.

Canaan is the land the LORD swore to the fathers and gives to the Israelites as an inheritance. The spies report it flows with milk and honey, and Joshua and Caleb call it exceedingly good, though its peoples (Amalek, Hittite, Jebusite, Amorite, Canaanite) live in large fortified cities. Israel's adults reject it, so that generation, except Caleb and Joshua, will not see it; their little ones will enter. Later, Israel prepares to cross the Jordan to subdue it, Reuben and Gad promise to cross armed, and the king of Arad hears of Israel's coming. The account ends with the land's borders set on all four sides, including the great sea to the west, for division among the nine tribes and the half-tribe.

is_named_for cluster of grapes (Eshcol) [cut down by the Israelites] The spies come to the valley of Eshcol and cut down a branch with one cluster of grapes, carried on a staff between two men, along with pomegranates and figs. The place is named Eshcol because of the cluster the Israelites cut down there.
Kadesh is a city in the wilderness of Zin at Edom's border, where the Israelites stay and Miriam dies; Moses sends messengers to Edom from there, then Israel departs for Mount Hor.

The Jordan is the boundary between the eastern land Reuben and Gad want and the land of Canaan. The two tribes ask not to be brought over it, but then agree that their armed men will cross it before the LORD and keep their inheritance on the east side.
Children of Anak, including Ahiman, Sheshai and Talmai at Hebron, are described by the spies as Nephilim descendants of great stature, evidence of the land's strength.

dwells_in hill country The Amorites, under King Sihon, refuse Israel passage and fight them, and Israel strikes them down and takes their land from the Arnon to the Jabbok. Israel lives in their cities, and later drives out the Amorites at Jazer.

The Canaanites are a people dwelling by the sea, along the Jordan, in the valley with the Amalekites, and in the mountain; after Moses warns Israel, they descend and beat the Israelites down to Hormah.

lasts forty days The expedition goes up by the South into the hill country, passing from the wilderness of Zin to Rehob near Hamath, and through Hebron and Eshcol. It lasts forty days and ends with the return to Kadesh, where the spies report to Moses, Aaron, and the congregation.
A branch bearing one cluster of grapes is cut at the valley of Eshcol and carried on a staff between two men. It is shown to the congregation as fruit of the land and gives the valley its name.

is_given_by the twelve spies [the men who went up with Caleb] The men who went up with Caleb bring an evil report to the Israelites, saying they cannot go up against the stronger people and that the land eats up its inhabitants. They add that the people are of great stature, including the Nephilim, and that the spies seemed like grasshoppers in their own sight and in the sight of those people.

The people wish they had died in the wilderness, and the LORD decrees that their dead bodies will fall and be consumed there. Their children will wander in it forty years, and the people are told to turn toward it by the way to the Red Sea. The LORD's signs were also worked in the wilderness.

dwells_in valley [together with the Canaanite] The Amalekite is said to dwell in the valley, which is why the LORD tells the people to turn toward the wilderness. Moses warns that the Amalekite and Canaanite are before them. The Amalekites come down and strike the presumptuous Israelites, beating them to Hormah.

l: Israelites' rebellion and punishment of forty years, Numbers
s: The congregation complains, refuses to enter the land, and tempts the LORD ten times. The LORD sentences all counted adults twenty and older to die in the wilderness, except Caleb and Joshua. Their children wander forty years, a year per spying day. A later attempt to go up without the LORD ends in defeat.

The stranger living as a foreigner among Israel shares the same standing before the Lord under one eternal statute, offers fire offerings like natives, is forgiven with the congregation for unwitting sin, but is cut off for high-handed sin.

l: offerings by fire (burnt offerings, sacrifices), Numbers
s: produces pleasant aroma to the LORD Offerings of the herd or flock, made as burnt offerings, sacrifices, vows, free will offerings, or at set feasts, must be accompanied by fine flour mixed with oil and a wine drink offering. The amounts scale by animal: one tenth of an ephah of flour with a fourth of a hin of oil and wine for a lamb, two tenths with a third of a hin for a ram, and three tenths with half a hin for a bull. They are described as a pleasant aroma to the LORD.

Provisions for unwitting sin and atonement: a congregation that errs unwittingly offers a young bull burnt offering with meal and drink offerings plus a male goat sin offering; an individual offers a year-old female goat. The priest's atonement brings forgiveness, but defiant sinners despising the LORD's word are cut off.
A man found gathering sticks on the Sabbath in the wilderness is brought to Moses, Aaron, and the congregation, held in custody without a penalty, and then sentenced to death by the LORD.

l: stoning of the Sabbath breaker, Numbers
s: takes_place outside the camp [carried out by all the congregation] The LORD declares that the man shall surely be put to death by the whole congregation stoning him outside the camp. The congregation brings him out and stones him to death, as the LORD commanded Moses.

Fringes with a blue cord are worn on garment borders by the children of Israel throughout their generations, commanded by the LORD in Chapter 15. They serve as a visible reminder to obey all commandments, not follow their own hearts and eyes, and be holy.

purpose holiness to God [for Israel] The LORD's commandments given through Moses are to be observed from the day they were given and throughout the generations, and failure to observe them unwittingly requires sin offerings. Deliberately breaking his commandment with a high hand brings being cut off, and the fringes are given so the people will remember and do all of them.

Korah, a Levite son of Izhar, leads a challenge against Moses and Aaron claiming the whole congregation is holy; rebuked for seeking priesthood, he assembles the people and is swallowed alive by the earth with his household.

Dathan, son of Eliab of the tribe of Reuben, joins Korah's rebellion against Moses, refuses his summons, accuses him of leading them to die and claiming princeship, and is swallowed alive with his family at his tent door.

Abiram, Eliab's son of the tribe of Reuben, joins Korah's rebellion against Moses, refuses Moses's summons with Dathan, complains about the missing inheritance, and is swallowed alive with his household into Sheol.

destroyed_by earth swallowing the rebels [Korah's men and households] Korah's company, including the 250 princes of renown, gathers against Moses and Aaron and takes censers with fire and incense to stand before the LORD at the Tent of Meeting. The earth swallows Korah's men with their households and goods. Fire from the LORD devours the 250 men who offered incense.

Bronze censers carried by the 250 rebels and Aaron, with fire and incense, before the LORD. After the rebels' destruction, the censers were declared holy, beaten into altar-covering plates as a memorial; Aaron's censer later made atonement during the plague.

sends_to Sheol [Korah's people go down alive] As Moses finishes saying that the LORD would make a new thing, the ground splits and the earth opens its mouth. It swallows Korah's men, Dathan, Abiram, their households, and all their goods, who go down alive into Sheol before the earth closes over them. The Israelites around them flee at their cry for fear of being swallowed too.

A plague sent by the LORD's wrath after the congregation complained that Moses and Aaron killed the LORD's people; it kills 14,700, beyond Korah's dead, until Aaron's incense atonement between dead and living stops it.

Korah, Dathan, Abiram, On, and 250 princes challenge Moses and Aaron, claiming the whole congregation is holy. The earth swallows the leaders' households and fire consumes the incense offerers; censers become an altar covering, and further complaint brings a plague.

Aaron's rod, inscribed with Aaron's name to represent Levi's house, is laid up before the LORD overnight among others, then sprouts, buds, blossoms and bears ripe almonds. It is placed back before the covenant as a token against the children of rebellion.
Twelve rods, one per prince by father's house, are laid up before the covenant in the Tent of Meeting; only Aaron's rod buds, and the rest are returned to their owners.

l: murmuring and complaining of the Israelites, Numbers
s: is_directed_against Moses [also against the LORD] The LORD intends the budding of the chosen rod to make the Israelites' murmurings against Moses cease. He says Aaron's rod is to be kept as a token to end their complaining so that they not die, and the people respond with fear of perishing.

is_given_to Aaron's sons [also daughters; portion forever; eaten by the clean in the house] The wave offerings of the children of Israel are given to Aaron, his sons, and his daughters as a portion forever, a covenant of salt, and may be eaten by everyone clean in the house. The Levites in turn must offer a wave offering of the tithe they receive, a tithe of the tithe, to the LORD by giving it to Aaron.

The holy things of the children of Israel, including the most holy offerings from the fire, are given to Aaron and his sons by reason of the anointing. The Levites are warned not to profane the holy things, lest they die.

is_given_to Levites [by the LORD, from Israel as an inheritance] The LORD gives all the tithe in Israel to the Levites as their inheritance in return for their service at the Tent of Meeting. The Levites must offer a tithe of it, its best part, as the LORD's wave offering to Aaron, after which the remainder is credited to them like threshing floor grain and wine press increase and may be eaten anywhere.

The red heifer is a ritual animal required to be red, spotless, and never yoked. Given to Eleazar the priest, it is killed outside the camp, its blood sprinkled seven times toward the Tent of Meeting, then burned whole with cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet.

The ashes of the heifer are a sin offering, gathered by a clean man who becomes unclean until evening. They are stored in a clean place outside the camp and kept for the Israelite congregation, to be mixed with running water for cleansing impurity.

Water for impurity is made by pouring running water over ashes of the burnt sin offering in a vessel. A clean person sprinkles it with hyssop on the third and seventh days; touching it, or sprinkling it, makes one unclean until evening.

Corpse uncleanness is a seven-day impurity from touching a dead person, slain person, bone, grave, or being in a tent where someone dies. It spreads to open vessels and to things the unclean person touches until evening. Purification with water on the third and seventh days is required; otherwise the tabernacle is defiled and the person is cut off from Israel.

A perpetual statute binding the children of Israel and the resident stranger, governing purification from uncleanness through contact with the dead. The unclean person is sprinkled with the water for impurity on the third and seventh days, washes clothes, bathes, and is clean at evening. Those handling the heifer's ashes also become unclean until evening. Refusal brings being cut off for defiling the sanctuary. After battle, killers and touchers camp outside seven days with captives; garments, skin, goats' hair, and wood are purified, fireproof metals pass through fire and water, others through water, and clothes are washed on day seven.

Edom is a kingdom ruled by a king and described as Israel's brother; it is destined to become Israel's possession, yet it twice refuses Israel passage, threatens the sword, and confronts Israel with force, so Israel turns away.
Mount Hor, at the border of Edom, is where the Israelites arrive after leaving Kadesh; the LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron, and Aaron dies on its top after Eleazar receives his garments.

l: waters of Meribah of Kadesh, Numbers
s: Waters of Meribah in the wilderness of Zin: where Israel strove with the LORD and he was sanctified, later cited by the LORD as where Moses and Aaron rebelled against his word.
The LORD tells Moses to speak to the rock before the people's eyes so it will pour out water. Moses instead strikes it twice with his rod, and water comes out abundantly.

The lack of water for the congregation prompts the people's complaint against Moses and Aaron. Water comes out abundantly from the rock, and the congregation and their livestock drink. Israel also promises Edom to pay for any water they drink along the highway.

God, called the LORD, is the deity who swore land to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. He warns Balaam not to curse blessed Israel, permits him to go only speaking God's word, then angers at his going and sets an angel against him. Later he is recalled striking eastern lands and, in anger, condemning the Egypt generation, except Caleb and Joshua, to forty wandering years.
sent_by LORD [among the people as judgment] The LORD sends venomous snakes among the people as punishment for speaking against God and Moses. They bite the people, and many people of Israel die.
Bronze serpent Moses made and set on a pole at the LORD's instruction; anyone bitten by a serpent who looks at it lives.

fears Israel [because they were many] Moab is very afraid and distressed because of Israel's multitude, and its king Balak consults with the elders of Midian. Moab's elders and princes carry rewards of divination to Balaam and come back with a second delegation after he first refuses. Moab hopes to defeat Israel and drive them out of the land.

l: Sihon king of the Amorites, Numbers
s: Sihon, Amorite king ruling from Heshbon, earlier seized Moab's former king's land up to the Arnon. He refused Israel passage, fought them at Jahaz, and was struck down by the sword, losing his land.

is_a city of Sihon [taken by Israel, which lived in it and its villages] Heshbon is the city of Sihon king of the Amorites, and Israel lives in it and its villages after defeating him. A proverbial song says a fire went out from Heshbon and devoured Ar of Moab, and that Heshbon later perished as far as Dibon.

is_a king of Bashan Og, king of Bashan, goes out with all his people to battle Israel at Edrei. The LORD tells Moses not to fear him, and Israel strikes him, his sons, and his people until none survive, and possesses his land.

l: Balaam the son of Beor, Numbers
s: Balaam, son of Beor, is a seer from Pethor by the River in Aram, who hears the words of God and describes himself as one whose eyes are open. Balak says whomever Balaam blesses is blessed and whomever he curses is cursed, and summons him to curse Israel. Balaam consults God, who first forbids and then permits him to go if he speaks only God's word. He tells the envoys he cannot go beyond the LORD's word even for a house full of silver and gold. On the road he strikes his donkey three times, is rebuked by the LORD's angel, confesses 'I have sinned,' and is told to speak only what he is given. At Balak's high places he builds altars and makes offerings at three sites, but refuses to curse Israel, saying God has not cursed them and he cannot reverse the blessing. He wishes to die the death of the righteous. Seeing the LORD is pleased to bless Israel, he abandons divination, the Spirit of God comes on him, and he speaks parables blessing Israel and foretelling its future, with short oracles on Amalek and the Kenite. He then returns to his place.

Balak, son of Zippor, is king of Moab and an enemy of Israel. Fearing them, he sends messengers, then more honorable princes, to bring Balaam from Aram to curse Israel, promising great honor. He meets Balaam, sacrifices, and builds altars at high places, then moves him to Pisgah and Peor hoping for a different outcome. Balaam blesses instead each time. Balak finally says neither curse nor bless, then angrily strikes his hands together, tells Balaam to flee, says the LORD kept him from honor, and after Balaam's last oracles goes his own way.

The Midianites are a people whom the LORD commanded Moses to harass and strike for deceiving Israel at Peor and through Cozbi, who was slain with Zimri. Israel later attacks them, killing every male including five kings, burning cities and encampments, and taking women, children, livestock, and goods.

serves God [the LORD's angel] The LORD's angel stands in Balaam's way as an adversary with a drawn sword, three times, in the path, in a narrow path between walls, and in a narrow place with no room to turn. After Balaam's eyes are opened, the angel rebukes him for striking the donkey, says Balaam's way is perverse, and says he would have killed Balaam and spared the donkey. He then tells Balaam to go with the men but speak only what he is told.

Balaam's female donkey perceives the angel of the LORD before Balaam can. She turns aside, crushes his foot, and lies down, being struck each time. The LORD opens her mouth to protest; the angel says her turning saved Balaam's life.
The plains of Moab, by the Jordan near Jericho, stretch from Beth Jeshimoth to Abel Shittim, the journey's final encampment, where the LORD instructs Moses about taking Canaan.

desired_by Balak the son of Zippor [so he could strike and drive them out] Balak seeks a curse on Israel through Balaam so that Moab may strike them and drive them out. God forbids it, declaring Israel blessed, and Balaam repeatedly affirms he can speak only the word God gives. By the end of the unit Balaam has been brought to the high places of Baal and sees part of the people, but no curse has yet been spoken.

has_count seven Seven altars are built at Balaam's request at the first place, again at Pisgah, and a third set at Peor. On each altar a bull and a ram are offered, as a setting for Balaam to meet God.

consists_of a bull and a ram [per altar] A bull and a ram are offered on each of the seven altars at each of the places. Balak stands by his burnt offering with the princes of Moab while Balaam goes off to meet God. At Peor, Balaam again requests seven bulls and seven rams, and Balak offers them.

Balak asks Balaam to curse and defy Jacob and Israel, and tries from different places where Balaam may see only part of them. Balaam says he cannot curse whom God has not cursed, and that there is no enchantment or divination against Israel. Balak finally tells him neither to curse nor bless them.

Balaam blesses Israel instead of cursing, which Balak calls blessing them altogether. He says he has received a command to bless, that God has blessed and he cannot reverse it, and that it will be said of Jacob and Israel, 'What has God done!'

Balaam delivers two main parables, each opened with the formula that the man whose eyes are open speaks. The first blesses Israel's tents, prosperity, king, and strength, while the second looks to the latter days, with a star and scepter from Jacob conquering Moab, Edom, and Seir. Three shorter parables follow, announcing destruction for Amalek, the Kenite, and Asshur and Eber, the last of which says ships from Kittim will afflict them.

Baal Peor is the god to whom Israel joined itself at Shittim, which kindled the LORD's anger. Moses ordered that those who had joined themselves to Baal Peor be killed, and the Midianites are later blamed for deceiving Israel in the matter of Peor.

Phinehas, priest Eleazar's son and Aaron's grandson, stands from the congregation and spears Zimri and Cozbi, ending the plague. The LORD, citing his jealousy, credits him with atoning for Israel and grants him a covenant of peace and everlasting priesthood for his offspring.
Zimri, son of Salu and a Simeonite prince of a fathers' house, brazenly brought a Midianite woman, Cozbi, to his brothers before Moses and the congregation, and Phinehas killed him along with her.

Cozbi, a Midianite woman and daughter of Zur, a Midianite leader, was brought by Zimri, then killed by Phinehas on the day of the plague; the LORD cited this incident as grounds for striking the Midianites.

A census commanded by the LORD and carried out by Moses and Eleazar on the plains of Moab by the Jordan at Jericho. It counts Israelite men twenty and older able to war, by tribe and family, totaling 601,730, to guide land division; only Caleb and Joshua survive from the Sinai count.

Zelophehad, son of Hepher of Manasseh's families, died in the wilderness in his own sin, not as part of Korah's company, leaving no sons. His daughters, including Mahlah, were granted his inheritance by the LORD's command, and their marriages were arranged to keep it within their father's tribal family.

Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah are the five daughters of Zelophehad. They came before Moses, Eleazar, the princes and the congregation, arguing their father's name should not be lost for lack of a son, and the LORD declared they speak right, granting them their father's inheritance. Later, concern arose that marriage might transfer it, so they were commanded to marry within their tribe and married their father's brothers' sons in Manasseh.

Land inheritance by lot is the LORD's method for dividing the land among Israel's tribes. In Chapter 26 it is apportioned by number of names, with larger tribes receiving more and smaller ones less, assigned by lot according to fathers' tribal names, while Levites get none. Chapter 33 repeats the command: lot by families and tribes, larger groups larger shares, and wherever the lot falls is the man's.

A statute and ordinance for the children of Israel, established by the LORD in Chapter 27, setting the order of inheritance when a man dies without a son: first to his daughter, then his brothers, then his father's brothers, and finally his nearest kinsman.
At the LORD's command, Moses commissions Joshua by laying hands on him before Eleazar and the congregation, giving him authority to be obeyed, with Eleazar inquiring for him by the Urim.

The continual burnt offering is two year-old unblemished male lambs offered daily with fine flour, beaten oil and a drink offering. Ordained at Mount Sinai as a pleasing aroma to the LORD, it underlies all Sabbath, monthly and festival offerings.

l: morning and evening lambs (continual burnt offering), Numbers
s: The continual burnt offering consists of one unblemished year-old male lamb offered each morning and another at evening. Each is accompanied by a tenth ephah of fine flour mixed with a fourth hin of beaten oil, plus a fourth hin drink offering poured out in the holy place.

The meal offering is fine flour mixed with oil, presented alongside burnt offerings. Amounts scale by animal: one tenth ephah per lamb, two tenths per ram, three tenths per bull; the Sabbath's two lambs take two tenths, and the daily offering uses a fourth of a hin of beaten oil.

measure_per_lamb fourth part of a hin [continual offering; strong drink poured in the holy place] The drink offering accompanies the burnt offerings: a fourth of a hin of strong drink for each daily lamb, poured in the holy place. For the monthly offering it is half a hin of wine for a bull, a third of a hin for the ram, and a fourth of a hin for a lamb.

The Sabbath offering is a burnt offering made every Sabbath: two unblemished year-old male lambs, with two tenths of an ephah of oil-mixed fine flour as meal offering, plus a drink offering, presented in addition to the continual burnt offering.

The monthly new moon offering is a burnt offering made at the start of each month: two young bulls, one ram, and seven unblemished year-old male lambs, with fine flour meal offerings mixed with oil and wine drink offerings scaled by animal. One male goat is added as a sin offering, alongside the continual burnt offering.

The Feast of Unleavened Bread begins on the fifteenth day of the first month and lasts seven days, during which unleavened bread is eaten. The first and seventh days are holy convocations with no regular work. Daily offerings are two young bulls, one ram, seven male lambs, and a male goat as sin offering.

The Feast of Weeks, also called the day of the first fruits, is a observance when a new meal offering is brought to the LORD. It features a holy convocation without regular work, and an offering of two young bulls, a ram, seven male lambs, and a goat for atonement, all without defect, besides the continual burnt offering.

The Feast of Trumpets is a day of blowing of trumpets held on the first day of the seventh month. It is a holy convocation with no regular work. It requires a burnt offering of one young bull, one ram, and seven male lambs, plus a male goat as a sin offering for atonement.

The Day of Atonement is a holy convocation on the tenth day of the seventh month. People must afflict their souls and do no work. Required offerings are a young bull, a ram, seven male lambs, and a male goat as a sin offering, in addition to the atonement sin offering and continual burnt offering.

The Feast of Tabernacles is a seven-day feast to the LORD beginning on the fifteenth day of the seventh month with a holy convocation, when regular work is prohibited. Each day requires two rams, fourteen male lambs, and one male goat as a sin offering. The bull offerings decrease daily, from thirteen on the first day down to seven on the seventh day.

A solemn assembly on the eighth day after the seven-day feast, forbidding regular work. Its reduced offerings are a burnt offering of one bull, one ram, seven male lambs, plus a male goat sin offering, with meal and drink offerings.

A burnt offering is an offering made by fire to the LORD as a pleasant aroma. Chapter 29 prescribes bulls, rams and unblemished yearling lambs for each holy day, with meal and drink offerings, beyond the continual burnt offering.

purpose atonement One male goat is required as a sin offering on each of the holy days, beginning with the first day, where it is to make atonement for the people. It is always given in addition to the continual burnt offering, and on the tenth day also in addition to the sin offering of atonement.

l: woman (young, in her father's house), Numbers
s: lives_in father's house [in her youth] A young woman living in her father's house who vows a vow or binds herself by a pledge has her vows stand if her father hears and says nothing. If her father forbids her on the day he hears, none of her vows stand and the LORD will forgive her.
A father whose young daughter lives in his house; when he hears her vows and pledges, his silence upholds them, but forbidding her on the same day he hears makes them void.

The husband is a figure of authority over his wife's vows and binding oaths, and over a young woman's vows in her father's house. Silence on the day he hears establishes them; forbidding that day voids them. If he nullifies them after hearing, he bears her iniquity.

Vows are promises made to the LORD by a man or woman. A man must keep his word and never break it; a woman's vows stand or fall by her father's or husband's silence or prohibition on the day he hears, while a widow's or divorced woman's stand.

l: army of Israel (twelve thousand men of war), Numbers
s: A force of twelve thousand men, one thousand from each tribe, led by Phinehas, is sent against Midian. They kill every male, the five kings, and Balaam, burn the cities, and take captives and plunder. After purifying themselves for seven days outside camp, they pay a tax on their half; officers report no losses.

l: officers (captains of thousands and hundreds), Numbers
s: Officers, captains of thousands and hundreds, draw Moses' anger for saving the women alive; afterward they report no men missing and bring a gold offering to atone for their souls.

The women of Midian are taken captive with their little ones and blamed for the Peor incident through Balaam's counsel. Moses orders those who have known a man killed; thirty-two thousand girls who have not are spared as plunder.

The plunder is a large war booty of 675,000 sheep, 72,000 cattle, 61,000 donkeys and 32,000 persons, beyond what soldiers took themselves. It is split into two halves, warriors and congregation; one in five hundred of the warriors' half goes to the LORD, one in fifty of the congregation's to the Levites.

l: gold offering of the officers, Numbers
s: Gold offering from the captains of thousands and hundreds: ornaments, armlets, bracelets, rings, earrings, necklaces, given to atone for their souls. It weighs 16,750 shekels; Moses and Eleazar bring it into the Tent of Meeting as a memorial.
LORD commands vengeance on Midian; twelve thousand men with Phinehas, sanctuary vessels and trumpets fight, kill every male, burn cities, and return with captives and plunder, losing no Israelites.

Gilead is seen by Reuben and Gad as a place suited to livestock, and the two tribes plan to leave their families, flocks, and cities there. Moses conditionally grants it to them, and Machir son of Manasseh takes it, dispossesses the Amorites, and is given Gilead by Moses to live in.

The very great multitudes of livestock owned by Reuben and Gad are the stated reason for their request, since the land of Jazer and Gilead suits livestock. The tribes plan to build sheepfolds for them, and their livestock stay in the cities of Gilead while the men go to war.

l: Reubenite and Gadite land request, Numbers
s: Reuben and Gad ask Moses, Eleazar, and the princes for eastern land in Gilead as livestock possession instead of crossing the Jordan. After Moses's rebuke, it is granted on condition their armed men fight in Canaan's conquest; they agree, and receive it with half of Manasseh.

The coming conquest of Canaan is the war in which Reuben and Gad pledge to take part, crossing the Jordan armed before the LORD until enemies are driven out and the land subdued. Moses's rebuke refers to the earlier failure at Kadesh Barnea, when discouragement kept the earlier generation from entering. After the conquest, the two tribes would be free of obligation and return to their eastern land.

The journeys are listed as a series of departures and encampments from Rameses through Succoth, Marah, Elim, Sinai, Kadesh, Mount Hor, and Abarim to the plains of Moab. Moses wrote down the starting points by the LORD's commandment.

Israel's departure from Egypt began at Rameses on the fifteenth day of the first month, the day after the Passover, boldly and openly, while Egyptians buried firstborn the LORD struck and he judged their gods.

will_harass children of Israel [if not driven out, like pricks in eyes and thorns in sides] The inhabitants of Canaan are to be driven out before Israel, and their stone idols, molten images, and high places destroyed. If any are left, they will be like pricks in Israel's eyes and thorns in its sides and will harass Israel.

l: nine tribes and the half-tribe, Numbers
s: The nine tribes and the half-tribe are the ones to whom the LORD commands that the land of Canaan be given by lot. Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh have already received their inheritance beyond the Jordan at Jericho eastward, toward the sunrise.

The borders of the land are described on four sides. The west is the great sea. The north runs from the great sea to Mount Hor, the entrance of Hamath, Zedad, Ziphron and Hazar Enan. The east runs from Hazar Enan through Shepham, Riblah and the sea of Chinnereth, down the Jordan to the Salt Sea. The south runs from Zin by Edom, past Akrabbim, Kadesh Barnea, Hazar Addar and Azmon, to the brook of Egypt and the sea.

l: division of the land by lot, Numbers
s: allotted_to nine tribes and the half-tribe [by lot, as the LORD commanded] Moses tells the people that the land is to be inherited by lot, as the LORD commanded, for the nine tribes and the half-tribe. The LORD names Eleazar, Joshua, and one prince from each tribe as the men who will carry out the division.

number one per tribe [to divide the land for inheritance] The LORD instructs that one prince from each tribe be taken to help divide the land for inheritance. They are named as Caleb son of Jephunneh (Judah), Shemuel son of Ammihud (Simeon), Elidad son of Chislon (Benjamin), Bukki son of Jogli (Dan), Hanniel son of Ephod (Manasseh), Kemuel son of Shiphtan (Ephraim), Elizaphan son of Parnach (Zebulun), Paltiel son of Azzan (Issachar), Ahihud son of Shelomi (Asher), and Pedahel son of Ammihud (Naphtali).
Forty-eight Levite cities with surrounding pasture lands, comprising six cities of refuge and forty-two others, each tribe contributing in proportion to its inheritance size.

Pasture lands are land around a city for the Levites' livestock, possessions, and animals, extending one thousand cubits outward from the wall, measured two thousand cubits on each side with the city centered.

Six cities of refuge, among the forty-eight Levitical cities, are appointed after Israel crosses the Jordan: three beyond the Jordan and three in Canaan. They shelter Israelites, strangers, and foreigners who kill unintentionally from the avenger until they stand before the congregation for judgment.

The man slayer is someone who kills a person unwittingly and may flee to a city of refuge to avoid dying before judgment. If the congregation finds no intent, he must stay there until the high priest dies; outside its border the avenger may kill him without guilt. Afterward he may return to his land.

executes murderer [puts him to death when he meets him] The avenger of blood is to put a murderer to death when he meets him. He is not guilty of blood if he kills a man slayer found outside the border of his city of refuge, but the congregation protects the man slayer from him until judgment.

A murderer is one who kills with an iron, stone, or wooden weapon, or through hatred, ambush, or hostile striking. He must be executed by the avenger of blood on the testimony of multiple witnesses, and no ransom may spare him.

The congregation acts as judge between the striker and the avenger of blood by the stated ordinances; if the killing was unintentional, it delivers the slayer from the avenger and restores him to his city of refuge.

is_characterized_by absence of hostility [no enmity, no seeking harm] Killing is unintentional when a person shoves another suddenly without hostility, hurls something without lying in wait, or casts a stone without seeing him, and was not the victim's enemy or seeking his harm. Such a killer may flee to a city of refuge and receives judgment by the congregation rather than immediate death.

l: murder and blood pollution of the land, Numbers
s: Murder pollutes the land; only the murderer's blood can atone for blood shed there. Israel must not defile the land, since the LORD dwells among them, making bloodshed a matter of sacred responsibility.

l: heads of the fathers’ households of the family of the children of Gilead, Numbers
s: belongs_to Gilead [family of the children of Gilead] These men, of the family of Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh, come before Moses and the princes to raise a concern. They argue that the daughters' marriage to men of other tribes would remove the inheritance from their fathers' lot and add it to the other tribe, even at the jubilee. Moses affirms that they speak rightly.

rule no movement from tribe to tribe [each tribe keeps its own inheritance] The inheritance, allotted by lot to the tribes, is at risk of transferring between tribes through the marriage of Zelophehad's daughters, and the transfer would be permanent after the jubilee. The ruling establishes that no inheritance shall move from one tribe to another and that each tribe shall keep its own. Zelophehad's inheritance remains in the tribe of Manasseh.

is_commanded_by LORD [must be within father's tribe] The daughters are permitted to marry whom they think best, provided the husband is from the family of their father's tribe. Mahlah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Noah marry their father's brothers' sons, within the families of the sons of Manasseh, so their inheritance remains in their father's tribe.

This document is the book of Judges, a narrative of Israel's cycle of failure after Joshua's death. It opens with incomplete conquest: Judah and Simeon succeed, Caleb's daughter Achsah is given to Othniel, but most tribes fail to drive out the Canaanites. An angel at Bochim rebukes Israel, and the text sets out the pattern: a new generation forgets the LORD and serves Baal, the LORD hands Israel to oppressors, he raises a judge to save them, and Israel relapses when the judge dies. Remaining nations are left to test Israel. Judges follow in turn: Othniel defeats Cushan Rishathaim; Ehud kills Eglon of Moab; Shamgar strikes Philistines; Deborah and Barak defeat Sisera, with Jael killing him by a tent peg, celebrated in a victory song that names tribes that fought and those that held back. Gideon, called while Midian devastates Israel, destroys his father's Baal altar, tests God with a fleece, and with three hundred men, trumpets, pitchers and torches routs Midian, then kills the kings Zebah and Zalmunna. He refuses rule but makes an ephod that becomes a snare. His son Abimelech murders his seventy brothers, becomes king at Shechem, destroys the city, and dies when a woman drops a millstone on him, fulfilling Jotham's curse. After Tola and Jair, Israel is oppressed by Philistines and Ammonites; Jephthah, driven out by his kin and recalled as chief, vows to sacrifice whatever first meets him and his only daughter does. He fights Ephraim, whose men are identified by 'Shibboleth.' Ibzan, Elon and Abdon follow. Samson, a Nazirite born to Manoah's wife, marries a Philistine, uses a riddle, burns Philistine fields with foxes, kills a thousand with a jawbone, and is betrayed by Delilah, who learns his strength lies in his hair. Blinded and enslaved, he pulls down Dagon's temple pillars, killing more in death than in life. The final chapters, repeatedly noting there was no king and everyone did what was right in his own eyes, show moral collapse: Micah's idols and hired Levite priest are taken by Danites who conquer Laish; a Levite's concubine is raped and killed at Gibeah of Benjamin. Israel's tribes war on Benjamin, nearly destroying it, then take wives for the survivors by slaughtering Jabesh Gilead and seizing the daughters of Shiloh.

Judah is a tribal group, brother and ally of Simeon, chosen by the LORD to go up first against the Canaanites. With the LORD's help he defeats enemies at Bezek, takes Jerusalem, Hebron, Zephath (Hormah), Gaza, Ashkelon and Ekron, and drives out the hill country inhabitants, but cannot expel the valley people because of their iron chariots. He is later commanded to go first against Benjamin.

Simeon goes up with his brother Judah into Judah's lot after Judah proposes that they fight together and then go into Simeon's lot. He joins Judah in striking the Canaanites of Zephath and utterly destroying it, and the city is named Hormah.

The LORD is the God of Israel, presented throughout these records as a deity who acts in history: he brought Israel out of Egypt, the house of bondage, swore the land to their fathers, gave it to them, and made a covenant he promised never to break. The central pattern is a cycle. Israel does evil and serves other gods; the LORD, angry over idolatry, sells or delivers them to raiders and enemies such as Cushan Rishathaim, Eglon of Moab, Jabin, Midian, the Philistines and Ammonites. Israel cries out, and he grieves at their misery and raises up judges and saviors, is with each judge all his days, and puts his Spirit on figures like Othniel, Gideon, Jephthah and Samson. The story opens with the LORD choosing Judah and delivering the Canaanites into its hand, though Judah is stopped by iron chariots. Because Israel disobeyed, he declares he will not drive out the remaining inhabitants and instead leaves the nations to test whether Israel will keep his way. Deborah and Barak defeat Sisera at his word, and the song in Chapter 5 praises him as coming from Seir and Edom. With Gideon he reduces the army to three hundred so Israel cannot boast of its own strength, and sets the Midianites' swords against each other; Gideon says the LORD shall rule Israel, yet after Gideon dies Israel forgets him. He sends an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem and repays their wickedness. In Chapter 10, after recounting past rescues from Egyptians, Amorites, Ammonites, Philistines, Sidonians, Amalekites and Maonites, he says he will save them no more because they forsook him, but is moved when they put away foreign gods. He is witness and Judge between Jephthah and Ammon. With Samson, he sends an angel, blesses him, uses Samson's desire to seek occasion against the Philistines, gives him water at Lehi, departs from him unnoticed after the shaving, and strengthens him a last time. At the close he answers Israel's inquiries at Bethel, strikes Benjamin before Israel, and is the one before whom Israel weeps, swears oaths and keeps a yearly feast at Shiloh, with the people saying he made a breach in the tribes.

Israel is the people, also called the children of Israel, whose story in these records is a repeating cycle of faithfulness, lapse, oppression, crying out, and deliverance. After Joshua's death they ask the LORD who should go up first against the Canaanites. Once strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor instead of driving them out. They then live among the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites, intermarry with them, and forget the LORD. They serve the Baals, Asheroth and Ashtaroth, which provokes the LORD, and they are described as stubborn and as acting more corruptly than their fathers. They served the LORD through the days of Joshua and the elders who outlived him. After that they do evil again and again, and are handed to enemies: Cushan Rishathaim for eight years, Eglon for eighteen, Jabin for twenty, Midian, and the Philistines and Ammonites, with the Philistines holding them forty years. Each time they cry out and are saved by judges or deliverers: Othniel, Ehud, Deborah, Gideon and Jephthah. The land has rest for forty and eighty years at different points. Under Midian they are brought very low, hiding in dens, caves and strongholds. After Gideon, whom they asked to rule them, makes an ephod and dies, they turn to the Baals and Baal Berith and show his house no kindness. Tola and Jair lead them for stretches. Later they put away foreign gods, serve the LORD, and assemble at Mizpah. Jephthah recounts how the LORD gave them the Amorite land after Sihon, and they lived in Heshbon three hundred years. The final chapters note that there was no king in Israel. After the Levite's concubine is outraged, Israel assembles as one man, fights Benjamin at great cost, defeats it by ambush, and burns its cities. They then weep at Bethel at the loss of a tribe, build an altar, devise ways to give Benjamin wives without breaking their oath, and each man goes home to his own tribe and inheritance.

Joshua, son of Nun and servant of the LORD, dismisses the people to their inheritances; Israel serves the LORD throughout his life and the elders' who outlive him. He dies at 110 and is buried at Timnath Heres.

The Canaanites are struck down by Judah at Bezek and in the hill country, the South, and the lowland. Many remain in the land, living among Manasseh, Ephraim, Zebulun, Asher, and Naphtali, and some are put to forced labor.
Adoni-Bezek is a king in Bezek who mutilated seventy kings. Caught after fleeing, Judah's forces cut off his thumbs and big toes; he says God repaid him, and he is taken to Jerusalem, where he dies.

Caleb is a man, father of Achsah, with a younger brother Othniel. He offers Achsah to whoever takes Kiriath Sepher; Othniel does, Caleb blesses her with springs, receives Hebron, and drives out Anak's three sons.

Achsah, Caleb's daughter, is married to Othniel. On arrival she has him request a field, then herself asks Caleb for springs of water because he placed her in the South; Caleb gives upper and lower springs.

l: Othniel the son of Kenaz, The Book of Judges
s: Othniel, son of Kenaz and Caleb's younger brother, wins Achsah, Caleb's daughter, as wife by taking Kiriath Sepher (Debir). Later the LORD raises him up as Israel's savior; empowered by the LORD's Spirit, he judges Israel and defeats Cushan Rishathaim. The land rests forty years before he dies.
Ashkelon is where Samson goes down after the companions answer his riddle, with the LORD's Spirit on him. There he strikes thirty men and takes their plunder.

Benjamin is a tribe of Israel and brother to the other tribes, living in its inherited land alongside Jebusites it did not drive from Jerusalem. It refuses to hand over the wicked men of Gibeah and gathers twenty-six thousand swordsmen. After winning two days, it is crushed on the third, leaving only six hundred men at the rock of Rimmon, and its cities are burned. An oath cuts it off from Israel's daughters, and the people grieve. Offered peace, the survivors receive four hundred women of Jabesh Gilead, seize wives at Shiloh, and rebuild their cities.

l: house of Joseph, The Book of Judges
s: has_companion LORD [when going up against Bethel] The house of Joseph goes up against Bethel with the LORD's help and sends spies to scout it. They take the city with the edge of the sword after a man shows them the entrance, sparing the man and his family. Later their hand prevails over the Amorites, who become subject to forced labor.
Bethel, formerly called Luz, is a city spied out by the house of Joseph; an informant reveals its entrance and it is struck by the sword.

l: man from Bethel, The Book of Judges
s: A man from Bethel, spotted by watchers leaving the city, reveals its entrance in exchange for kind treatment. He and his family are spared, and he travels to the Hittites' land, builds a city, and names it Luz.

Ephraim is a hill-country region and its people, living alongside Canaanites in Gezer. Its men answer Gideon's call, taking the waters and killing the Midianite princes Oreb and Zeeb. Later they threaten Jephthah over not being called against Ammon, and are struck down by Gilead, with forty-two thousand falling.

l: angel of the LORD, The Book of Judges
s: A messenger of the LORD who appears twice. He first goes from Gilgal to Bochim, recalls the exodus and covenant, rebukes Israel for leaving altars standing and making covenants with the land's inhabitants, and announces the LORD will not drive them out; the people weep. Later he sits under the oak at Ophrah, commissions Gideon to save Israel, consumes an offering with fire from his staff, and vanishes.

l: inhabitants of the land (Canaanite nations), The Book of Judges
s: remain_as snare to Israel [left undriven by the LORD] Israel was told to make no covenant with the inhabitants of the land and to break down their altars, but did not obey. As a result the LORD says they will be in Israel's sides and their gods a snare. The LORD says he will no longer drive out the nations Joshua left, and leaves them to test Israel.

l: gods (foreign gods), The Book of Judges
s: The inhabitants' gods are foretold as a snare to Israel. The new generation follows and bows down to the gods of surrounding peoples, including Baal and the Ashtaroth, thereby provoking the LORD to anger. Israel's prostitution after other gods continues after each judge dies.
After Gideon's death, the children of Israel turn again and play the prostitute following the Baals. They make Baal Berith their god.

l: new generation (after Joshua's generation), The Book of Judges
s: A generation arising after Joshua's generation dies; it ignores the LORD and his work for Israel, then does evil, serves the Baals, abandons the LORD, and follows other gods.

l: judges (raised up by the LORD), The Book of Judges
s: saves Israel [from plunderers, raised up by the LORD] The LORD raises up judges who save Israel from those who plunder them, and he is with each judge and saves Israel all the days of that judge. Israel does not listen to the judges, and when a judge dies the people turn back and act more corruptly than their fathers.

l: raiders and enemies of Israel, The Book of Judges
s: The LORD delivers Israel into the hands of raiders who plunder them and sells them to enemies all around, so that Israel can no longer stand before them. The LORD's hand is against Israel wherever they go. The enemies oppress and trouble Israel until the LORD raises up judges to save them.

l: Israel's apostasy and oppression cycle, The Book of Judges
s: is_a recurring pattern [Israel turns back to corruption after each judge dies] The unit shows a pattern: Israel abandons the LORD for other gods, the LORD's anger burns and he gives them to plunderers, Israel groans, and he raises a judge who saves them. When the judge dies Israel relapses, becoming more corrupt than before. This leads the LORD to leave the remaining nations as a test of whether Israel will keep his way.

l: Cushan Rishathaim king of Mesopotamia, The Book of Judges
s: is_a king of Mesopotamia Cushan Rishathaim was the king into whose hand the LORD sold Israel because of their evil, and Israel served him eight years. The LORD delivered him into Othniel's hand, and Othniel's hand prevailed against him.

l: Eglon king of Moab, The Book of Judges
s: Eglon, very fat king of Moab, strengthened by the LORD, allied with Ammonites and Amalek, struck Israel, took the city of palm trees, ruled eighteen years, then Ehud killed him with a sword.

l: Ehud the son of Gera, The Book of Judges
s: Ehud, son of Gera, is a left-handed Benjamite raised up by the LORD as Israel's savior. He brings tribute to Eglon, kills him alone with a hidden self-made sword, escapes to Seirah, then rallies Israel with a trumpet in Ephraim to seize the Jordan fords and defeat Moab.

l: Shamgar the son of Anath, The Book of Judges
s: Shamgar, son of Anath, a savior of Israel who followed Ehud and killed six hundred Philistines with an ox goad.
Moab, a land bordered by the Arnon and ruled by King Eglon, oppressed Israel eighteen years until Ehud's Israelites seized the Jordan fords, killed about ten thousand Moabites, and subdued it.

The Philistines are an uncircumcised, Dagon-worshipping people who rule over Israel and Judah for forty years, delivered to them by the LORD. They are the main adversary of Samson, who is announced as the one to begin saving Israel from them. Samson's marriage among them provokes conflict: he strikes thirty men in Ashkelon, burns their grain and olive groves, and kills a thousand at Lehi. They retaliate by burning his wife and her father, then seize him through Delilah, blind him, and bind him in Gaza. Crediting Dagon, they summon him to entertain them, and he collapses the house, killing more of them in death than in life.

l: children of Ammon, The Book of Judges
s: The children of Ammon are an enemy people ruled by a king. With the Philistines they oppressed Israel for eighteen years, crossing the Jordan to attack Judah, Benjamin and Ephraim, then encamping in Gilead. They make war on Israel and ignore Jephthah's message. The LORD delivers them into his hand, and he strikes them with great slaughter across twenty cities, subduing them. Jephthah later recalls this strife and victory.
The Gileadites take the fords of the Jordan against the Ephraimites. Fugitives of Ephraim who try to cross are questioned and killed there if they fail the pronunciation test.

l: sword (Ehud's sword), The Book of Judges
s: Ehud's self-made, two-edged, cubit-long sword was hidden under his clothing on his right thigh, drawn with his left hand, and thrust into Eglon, handle following blade, left in him and emerging behind.

Deborah is a prophetess, wife of Lappidoth, who judges Israel from under her palm tree between Ramah and Bethel. She summons Barak, relays the LORD's command to attack Sisera, goes with him, and says honor will go to a woman. Later she sings with Barak, declaring she arose as a mother in Israel when rulers had ceased.

l: Barak the son of Abinoam, The Book of Judges
s: Barak, son of Abinoam of Kedesh Naphtali, is summoned by Deborah to lead ten thousand men to Mount Tabor. He agrees only if she accompanies him, pursues Sisera's army, and finds Sisera dead in Jael's tent. He later joins Deborah's victory song, leading captives away.

Sisera is captain of Jabin's army, living in Harosheth of the Gentiles. He gathers nine hundred iron chariots at the river Kishon against Barak, but his army is routed and swept away. He flees on foot to Jael's tent, asks for water, receives milk, and is killed in his sleep by a tent peg through his temples. His mother waits in vain at the window.

Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite, is a woman who welcomed fleeing Sisera into her tent, gave him milk, and killed him with a tent peg and hammer while he slept, then showed his body to Barak. The following chapter celebrates her as blessed above women.
