Jabin, king of Canaan reigning in Hazor, held Israel under his hand with Sisera as captain, kept peace with Heber's house, and was finally subdued by God and destroyed by Israel.

l: ten thousand men, The Book of Judges
s: A force of ten thousand men drawn from Naphtali and Zebulun, taken by Barak to Mount Tabor, summoned at Kedesh, then following him down from Tabor into battle against Sisera.

l: Sisera's army, The Book of Judges
s: has_commander Sisera Sisera's army, gathered with him from Harosheth of the Gentiles to the river Kishon, was confused by the LORD before Barak. It was pursued back to Harosheth of the Gentiles, and all of it fell by the sword, with not a man left.

l: chariots of iron (Sisera's chariots), The Book of Judges
s: has_quantity nine hundred Sisera had nine hundred chariots of iron, with which Jabin mightily oppressed Israel. Sisera gathered all of them to the river Kishon, where the LORD confused them before Barak, and Sisera abandoned his own chariot to flee.

l: hammer and tent peg (Jael's), The Book of Judges
s: Jael took a tent peg and a hammer and struck the peg into Sisera's temples as he slept deeply. It pierced through into the ground and killed him, and it was still in his temples when Barak saw the body.

l: battle at the river Kishon, The Book of Judges
s: The LORD had said he would draw Sisera and his chariots and multitude to the river Kishon, and Sisera gathered them there. Barak came down from Mount Tabor with ten thousand men, the LORD confused Sisera's forces, and the whole army fell by the sword while Sisera fled on foot. The kings of Canaan fought at Taanach by the waters of Megiddo and took no plunder of silver. The stars fought against Sisera, the river Kishon swept the enemy away, and horse hoofs stamped as their strong ones pranced.

l: men of Gilead, The Book of Judges
s: Men of Gilead, living beyond the Jordan, are gathered by Jephthah and strike Ephraim. They seize the Jordan fords, test crossers with 'Shibboleth', and kill those who fail, killing forty-two thousand Ephraimites.

l: song of Deborah and Barak, The Book of Judges
s: A victory song sung by Deborah and Barak, calling kings and princes to hear and blessing the LORD, praising willing leaders, recounting tribes that fought or stayed back, cursing Meroz, blessing Jael, and ending praying enemies perish.

Gideon, also called Jerub-Baal or Jerubbaal, is a man of Israel, son of Joash the Abiezrite, from Ophrah in Manasseh. He describes his family as the poorest in Manasseh and himself as the least in his father's house. The LORD's angel calls him a mighty man of valor and commissions him to save Israel from Midian. After receiving a sign, he builds an altar named "The LORD is Peace" and destroys Baal's altar and the Asherah by night, earning the name Jerub-Baal. Filled with the LORD's Spirit, he gathers Abiezer and several tribes, asks for fleece signs, and reduces his army to three hundred men. He leads the trumpet-and-pitcher attack on the Midianite camp, receives the heads of Oreb and Zeeb, placates Ephraim, and pursues Zebah and Zalmunna. He punishes Succoth and Penuel for refusing bread and kills the two kings in revenge for his brothers killed at Tabor. He refuses to rule Israel, saying the LORD shall rule, yet makes an ephod from gold that becomes a snare to him and his house. He has seventy sons by many wives, plus Abimelech by a concubine in Shechem, and Jether is his firstborn. He dies at a good old age and is buried in Ophrah in his father's tomb. Jotham later notes that his house was repaid with the killing of his sons despite his deliverance of Shechem.

Midian is a group of invaders that oppressed Israel for seven years, allied with the Amalekites and the children of the east. With countless men and camels like locusts, they destroyed the land's produce as far as Gaza and camped in the valley of Jezreel, at Moreh. The LORD promised Gideon he would strike them as one man. Terrified by trumpets, shouts and torches, they fled as their swords turned on each other, and their princes Oreb and Zeeb were killed. Gideon then struck the remaining fifteen thousand and captured and killed kings Zebah and Zalmunna. Midian was subdued and lifted its head no more, and the land had rest forty years.

Joash the Abiezrite, Gideon's father, owns the Ophrah oak, Baal's altar, the Asherah, and a second bull. When townsmen demand Gideon's death, he tells them Baal should contend for himself if he is a god, and Gideon is named Jerub-Baal that day.

is_worshipped_at altar of Baal Baal was worshiped with an altar and an Asherah belonging to Joash's household. When the altar was broken down, Joash argued that if Baal is a god he should contend for himself, and Gideon was named Jerub-Baal, meaning let Baal contend against him.

l: altar of Baal, The Book of Judges
s: has_state broken down [by Gideon at night] The altar of Baal belonged to Gideon's father and stood in the city. The LORD commanded Gideon to throw it down, and he did so by night with ten servants. The townsmen found it broken in the morning and demanded Gideon's death for it.
is_located_near altar of Baal The Asherah stood beside the altar of Baal that Joash had. Gideon cut it down at the LORD's command, and its wood was used for the burnt offering on the new altar.

l: second bull (Joash's bull), The Book of Judges
s: has_age seven years The second bull, seven years old, belonged to Joash, and the LORD told Gideon to take it. Gideon offered it as a burnt offering on the altar he built, using the wood of the Asherah.

l: altar to the LORD (built by Gideon), The Book of Judges
s: Gideon built an altar at Ophrah after seeing the angel, naming it The LORD is Peace; it still stands there. He later built another altar on the stronghold at the LORD's command, offering the second bull.

has_state dry while ground had dew [second test] Gideon put a fleece of wool on the threshing floor as a test of God's promise to save Israel by his hand. The first night it was wet with dew while the ground was dry, enough to wring out a bowl of water, and the second night, at Gideon's request, it was dry while the ground was wet with dew.

l: Midianite oppression, The Book of Judges
s: Midianite oppression was a seven-year punishment for Israel's evil, when Midian and allies raided after each sowing, destroyed crops and livestock, and drove Israel into caves, prompting cries to the LORD, a prophet's message, and Gideon's call.

l: three hundred men (Gideon's chosen men), The Book of Judges
s: Three hundred men, chosen by the LORD because they lapped water with their hands to their mouths, are the force through whom he promises to save Israel. Gideon divides them into three companies armed with trumpets and torch-filled pitchers, and they surround the Midianite camp for a night attack.

l: people (Israelite fighters with Gideon), The Book of Judges
s: number_after_first_reduction ten thousand [after twenty-two thousand returned] Of the people with Gideon, twenty-two thousand return home after the proclamation for the fearful, leaving ten thousand. The test at the water reduces these to three hundred, and the rest are sent to their tents after taking food and their trumpets.
killed_at Oreb’s rock [killed by Ephraim's men] Oreb is one of the two princes of Midian taken by the Ephraimites. He is killed at Oreb's rock, and his head is brought to Gideon beyond the Jordan.

killed_at Zeeb’s wine press [killed by Ephraim's men] Zeeb is one of the two princes of Midian taken by the Ephraimites. He is killed at Zeeb's wine press, and his head is brought to Gideon beyond the Jordan.

l: dream of the barley cake, The Book of Judges
s: A Midianite's dream of a barley cake tumbling into the camp and flattening a tent is told to his fellow, who interprets it as Gideon's sword and God's deliverance of Midian; Gideon overhears, worships, and rouses Israel.

l: test at the water, The Book of Judges
s: purpose select men to go with Gideon [lapping like a dog versus kneeling] At the LORD's direction Gideon brings the ten thousand down to the water, where those who lap with the tongue like a dog, putting a hand to the mouth, are set apart from those who bow on their knees to drink. Three hundred lap, and the LORD chooses them to save Israel while the rest are sent home.

has_leaders seventy-seven princes and elders The princes of Succoth refuse Gideon's request for bread for his faint men, mocking whether Zebah and Zalmunna are already in his hand. After the capture, Gideon learns from a young man the names of its princes and elders, seventy-seven men, and takes the elders and teaches the men of Succoth with thorns and briers.

is_a king of Midian Zebah, a king of Midian, is in Karkor with an army when Gideon strikes it; he flees, is captured, and is questioned about the men killed at Tabor. Gideon kills him along with Zalmunna after learning those men were his brothers.

is_a king of Midian Zalmunna, a king of Midian, is in Karkor with Zebah and flees but is captured by Gideon. He and Zebah say that as the man is, so is his strength, and Gideon kills them and takes the crescents from their camels' necks.

has_structure tower [broken down by Gideon] The men of Penuel answer Gideon's request for bread as Succoth did, and Gideon vows to break down their tower when he returns in peace. He later breaks down the tower of Penuel and kills the men of the city.

The ephod is an object Gideon made from collected gold earrings weighing 1,700 shekels and placed in Ophrah, his city; all Israel prostituted themselves with it, and it became a snare to Gideon's house.

Shechem is where Abimelech is made king by the oak of the pillar. Zebul drives Gaal out of it, and Abimelech fights against it all day, takes it, kills its people, beats it down, and sows it with salt.
